Learning Objectives
Recognize nonmodifiable and modifiable risk factors associated with total hip and knee
arthroplasty.
Identify risk factors that can be optimized to improve outcomes and minimize complications in
patients undergoing total hip or knee arthroplasty.
Review the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons evidence-based clinical practice
guidelines on the management of hip and knee osteoarthritis. (Resources 1 and 2)
Define the ideal patient for outpatient total joint arthroplasty.

Perioperative management of a patient undergoing total hip or total knee arthroplasty
encompasses the period around or near joint arthroplasty (Resource 3).
Patient Comorbidities and Hip and Knee Arthroplasty
Nonmodifiable risk factors—Age, sex, race, and medical comorbidities can be used to establish
patient and family expectations on the risk of readmission after total hip arthroplasty (THA) or
total knee arthroplasty (TKA).1
Increased age
Increased risk of mortality
Lower functional and quality-of-life outcomes
Race and underrepresented minority groups2,3
Higher risk for adverse outcomes after TKA
Higher risk for periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) after TKA
Higher risk for mortality after THA
Modifiable risk factors—Optimization of medical comorbidities may improve TJA outcomes.4
Diabetes mellitus
Higher rate of complications and increased risk for revision surgery after TKA
Patients with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus may have a higher risk for short-term
adverse events after THA.
Preoperative HbA1c levels higher than 6.7% are associated with an increased risk for
wound complications.
Perioperative acute hyperglycemia (fasting blood glucose level higher than 200 mg/dL) is
associated with an increased risk for wound complications.
The ideal preoperative HbA1c level remains unclear; however, a well-controlled blood
glucose level in the perioperative period is ideal and should be less than 8%.
Obesity
Consistently identified as a major risk factor for postoperative complications after TKA and
THA.
Increased risk for postoperative dislocation, superficial wound infection, and blood loss
after THA.
Although bariatric surgery decreases BMI, the effect on TJA outcomes remains unclear and
has not consistently resulted in a reduction in complications. To be effective, weight loss
must occur in a manner that avoids malnutrition.5

Patients with obesity who undergo THA or TKA report lower absolute outcome scores but
similar levels of patient satisfaction and relative improvement in pain and function.
A workgroup of the American Association of Hip and Knee Surgeons Evidence-Based
Committee concluded the following6:
Improvements occurred in patient-related outcome measures.
All patients with obesity (BMI >30 kg/m2) who undergo TJA have an increased risk for
perioperative complications.
Increased risks should be discussed with every patient with obesity.
The consensus opinion of the workgroup was that delayed TJA should be considered in a
patient with a BMI of 40 kg/m2, especially those with other comorbid conditions, such as
poorly controlled diabetes mellitus or malnutrition.
Smoking
Single most important risk factor for postoperative complications, particularly those related
to wound healing, cardiopulmonary complications, and the requirement for postoperative
intensive care.
Current smokers have a higher rate of complications compared with nonsmokers.
Increasing pack-year history of smoking results in an increasing total complication risk.
Smoking cessation program 6 to 8 weeks before TJA: complication rate of 52% in smokers
and 18% in patients who participated in the smoking cessation program.
Malnutrition
Malnutrition may play a more important role than obesity and BMI.
An albumin level less than 3.5 g/dL at the time of elective TJA is associated with higher risk for
surgical site infection (SSI), pneumonia, extended hospital length of stay, and hospital
readmission.
An albumin level less than 3.5 g/dL is a stronger and more consistent independent risk factor
for any complication, including wound, cardiac, or respiratory complications, and for death.
Cardiovascular disease
High risk factor for perioperative myocardial infarction and mortality after elective TJA.
Age older than 80 years, hypertension requiring medication, and history of cardiac disease
are substantial risk factors for cardiac complications within 30 days after TJA.
No evidence-based guidelines are available for the management of antiplatelet therapy
cessation and TJA.
Patients with coronary stents who require surgical treatment that mandates discontinuation
of treatment via anti-platelet agents should continue aspirin therapy and restart the

antiplatelet agent as soon as possible.
Patients should delay elective surgery at least 30 days for bare metal stents and as long as 6
months for drug-eluting stents. A patient’s cardiologist should be consulted before
proceeding with surgical treatment.
Preoperative cardiology evaluation and co-management in the perioperative period for
individuals with these risk factors is helpful.
Postoperative atrial fibrillation, myocardial infarction, and coronary artery disease are
independent variables predicting PJI after primary elective TJA.
Congestive heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Higher rates of revision THA within 12 months of the index arthroplasty
Independent risk factor for revision TKA within 12 months of primary TKA
Chronic renal disease
Inpatient mortality rates for dialysis-dependent patients are 10 to 20 times higher and overall
complication rates are two times higher than those for non–dialysis-dependent patients.
Harmful effect on long-term life expectancy in patients who undergo TJA and fewer quality-
adjusted life-years even if clinical outcomes are similar
Cirrhosis, hepatitis C
Higher complication rates reported after TJA
Higher complication rates, even if the patient does not have liver damage
Preoperative management of hepatitis C virus may decrease the risk for complications,
including PJI and revision TKA.7
Recommendation that hepatitis C virus treatment regimens should be integrated into the
preoperative TJA optimization protocol for this high-risk group of patients.
Opioid use
Chronic opioid use leading up to TJA results in a higher rate of revision surgery.8
Patients with chronic multiple joint, low back, or spine pain have poorer TKA outcomes.
A 50% reduction in opioids reduces the negative effects of opioid use.
Moderate evidence supports that patients with select chronic pain conditions experience less
improvement in patient-reported outcomes with TKA.
Poor dentition
The American Dental Association recommends good oral hygiene before and after TJA.
Dental clearance may be beneficial in high-risk patients only (tobacco use, history of tooth
extraction, older age, narcotic use, and lack of dental visit within 12 months).
Preoperative anemia

Preoperative anemia (<11 mg/dL) is associated with an increased risk for cardiac
complications, genitourinary complications, longer hospital length of stay, greater incidence
of PJI, and increased mortality.
Tranexamic acid considerably limits perioperative blood loss and decreases the need for
transfusions.
Other techniques for blood conservation include hypotensive anesthesia, red cell salvage,
topical fibrin sprays, and sealants.
Staphylococcus aureus colonization
Methicillin-resistant S aureus and methicillin-sensitive S aureus colonization have been shown
to result in a higher incidence of postoperative SSI among patients undergoing elective TJA.
Screening and nasal decolonization of S aureus may reduce the rates of staphylococcal SSI
after THA and TKA.
Methicillin-resistant S aureus and/or methicillin-sensitive S aureus nasal screening along with
a perioperative decolonization protocol have resulted in a 69% decreased SSI rate.
Decolonization treatment via a 5-day course of intranasal mupirocin (2%) twice per day has
been shown to be an effective method for eradicating colonization of S aureus.
Use of chlorhexidine baths for 3 to 5 days preoperatively also is recommended for
decolonization.
Another strategy to manage Staphylococcus colonization is universal decontamination.
Screening is not performed, and all patients are decolonized.
Universal decolonization has been shown to be less costly and effective.9
Povidone-iodine is an alternative to mupirocin that also has shown good results in
decolonization.10
Neurocognitive, psychological, and behavioral
Mental health disorders, such as depression, anxiety, and psychosis, are associated with
decreased function, pain relief, and quality-of-life outcomes after THA.
Pain after TKA correlates with increased preoperative anxiety levels.
Reducing preoperative anxiety improves postoperative recovery and satisfaction with the
surgical experience and reduces self-reported pain.

An increased risk for perioperative total joint arthroplasty (TJA) complications has been
reported in patients older than 75 years and in patients with uncontrolled diabetes
mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, high body mass index (BMI; >35 kg/m2),
chronic opioid use, functional neurologic impairments, dependent functional status, low
preoperative cognitive capacity, congestive heart failure, liver cirrhosis, or chronic kidney
disease.
Anesthesia
Periarticular anesthesia
Strong evidence supports the use of periarticular local anesthetic infiltration during TKA to
decrease pain and opioid use.
Peripheral nerve blockade
Strong evidence supports the use of peripheral nerve blockade during TKA to decrease
postoperative pain and opioid requirements.
Neuraxial anesthesia
Moderate evidence supports the use of neuraxial anesthesia during TKA to improve
outcomes and reduce complication rates compared with general anesthesia.
Some evidence suggests that, compared with general anesthesia, the use of neuraxial
anesthesia reduces complications in patients with symptomatic osteoarthritis of the hip
undergoing THA, including the following11:
Postoperative nausea
Blood transfusions
SSIs
Non-home discharges
Postoperative Management
The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons evidence-based clinical practice guidelines
on the management of hip and knee osteoarthritis (Resources 4 and 5)
Cryotherapy devices
No improvement in outcomes after TKA
May improve range of motion during inpatient hospital stay
Continuous passive motion

No improvement in outcomes after TKA
Physical therapy
Preoperative physical therapy
No improvement in pain control or physical function after TJA
Postoperative physical therapy
Started on the day of surgery reduces pain, improves function, and decreases hospital
length of stay for TKA and THA
Inpatient Admission
The medical conditions listed in Table 1 must be assessed carefully.12

If these medical conditions are present, they may increase the risk for complications or
adverse events, and inpatient admission may occur.
Discharge on the day of TJA is associated with higher risk for cardiac and pulmonary
complications compared with discharge on postoperative day one.
Obtaining appropriate clearance before surgical management is critical.
Certain individuals with considerable cardiopulmonary risks are not candidates for same
day/outpatient TJA ( Resource 6).
